Improving the Expressive Power of Hybrid Sequence Models via Multi-Hop Retrieval

Yam Eitan Affiliation: Technion – Israel Institute of Technology    Gilad Yehudai Affiliation: Technion – Israel Institute of Technology    Haggai Maron Affiliation: Technion – Israel Institute of Technology Affiliation: NVIDIA
April 2026
Abstract

Hybrid architectures offer a promising approach to efficient language modeling by combining a small number of full-attention layers with a larger number of efficient sequence layers, such as sparse attention and recurrent layers. While full-attention layers maintain a KV cache that grows linearly with sequence length, efficient layers typically rely on separate, fixed-size states rather than accessing this richer existing memory. Recent work has begun exploring ways to allow efficient layers access to the KV cache, but the theoretical benefits of such access, and the extent to which existing approaches can realize them remain poorly understood. We investigate these questions by analyzing the expressive power of individual hybrid blocks on function composition, a well-studied task in sequence-model expressivity associated with multi-hop reasoning. We first establish that both conventional hybrid blocks and those with top-κ\kappa KV-cache access require Ω⁡(n)\Omega(\sqrt{n}) capacity to compute even two-function composition over a domain of size nn. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Multi-hop Retrieval Attention (MuRA) hybrid block, a simple architecture that enables multi-hop retrieval from a shared KV cache while preserving asymptotic computational and memory efficiency. We prove that a single fixed size mm-hop MuRA block can compute mm-function composition, whereas computing (m+1)(m+1)-function composition with the same retrieval depth requires polynomial model size, establishing a strict expressivity hierarchy in retrieval depth. Synthetic experiments support this hierarchy, showing that increasing retrieval depth enables learning progressively deeper compositions, substantially outperforming existing hybrid architectures. Together, our results identify multi-hop retrieval as a promising mechanism for improving the expressive power of efficient hybrid architectures.

1 Introduction

Transformers have become the dominant architecture for language modeling, but their computational and memory costs pose increasing challenges as models and context lengths grow. Full attention requires quadratic computation in sequence length and, during autoregressive inference, stores previously computed keys and values to avoid recomputation. Specifically, each attention layer maintains a key–value (KV) cache 𝑲=[𝒌1,…,𝒌n]{\bm{K}}=[{\bm{k}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{k}}_{n}] and 𝑽=[𝒗1,…,𝒗n]{\bm{V}}=[{\bm{v}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{v}}_{n}], consisting of a key and value vector for each preceding token. The memory required by this cache grows linearly with the context length, becoming a major bottleneck for long-context inference [50; 23; 44; 14]. These costs have motivated the development of efficient sequence layers, including sparse and local attention mechanisms [7; 2; 48] and, more recently, efficient recurrent layers  [19; 18; 46]. Recurrent layers process sequences in linear time and, during autoregressive inference, maintain only a fixed-size hidden state 𝒉n{\bm{h}}_{n} that summarizes the preceding context. Despite these efficiency gains, models relying exclusively on efficient sequence layers often underperform full-attention transformers on long context tasks [42; 35].

Nevertheless, recurrent layers have found considerable success in hybrid architectures. These architectures are typically organized into repeating hybrid blocks, each combining a single full-attention layer with several recurrent layers, reducing the frequency of expensive attention operations. This design has been adopted by prominent models such as Kimi K3 [40], Gemma 3 [16], Nemotron 3 Ultra [3], and OLMo Hybrid [27], demonstrating its effectiveness at scale. However, recurrent layers were originally designed to operate independently of full attention. Consequently, even within a hybrid block, they typically maintain their own fixed-size hidden states 𝒉t{\bm{h}}_{t}, without direct access to the richer KV cache already maintained by the full-attention layer. This raises a natural question: can recurrent layers benefit from direct access to this existing memory without sacrificing their computational efficiency? Recent work has begun exploring this possibility. Some approaches [5; 34] share KV caches across layers or apply attention to a subset of past recurrent states, reducing memory requirements but retaining quadratic attention computation. In contrast, other methods [13; 43] reuse a full-attention layer’s KV cache for sparse top-κ\kappa retrieval based on its attention scores, allowing subsequent layers to access shared memory without increasing the asymptotic time or memory complexity of hybrid blocks. While these methods have shown promising empirical results, their designs remain largely empirically motivated, with limited theoretical understanding of how different memory-access mechanisms affect model capabilities.

We aim to provide a principled foundation for designing such layers by investigating whether shared-memory access can improve the expressive power of hybrid blocks, and whether existing retrieval mechanisms fully realize this potential. Expressivity is particularly relevant in this setting: computations that can be realized within a single block of one architecture may require several blocks of another, introducing additional expensive full-attention operations and KV caches. More expressive blocks could therefore enable more efficient hybrid architectures.

Our analysis focuses on function composition, a well-studied task in sequence-model expressivity [33; 22; 47] that requires successive dependent retrievals, as often arise in multi-hop reasoning. We establish a fundamental expressive limitation shared by both conventional hybrid blocks with independent recurrent states and those whose recurrent layers access a shared KV cache through top-κ\kappa retrieval. Specifically, we prove that both require size Ω⁡(n)\Omega(\sqrt{n}), measured by the product of width, depth, and precision, to compute even two-function composition over a domain of size nn.

Motivated by this limitation, we introduce Multi-Hop Retrieval Attention (MuRA), which extends top-κ\kappa retrieval to provide efficient sequence layers with richer access to the full-attention layer’s KV cache. As in top-κ\kappa hybrid blocks, MuRA first identifies each token’s highest-scoring causal predecessors using the full-attention scores. However, rather than retrieving only the immediate predecessors of a query token, (κ1,…,κm)(\kappa_{1},\ldots,\kappa_{m})-MuRA recursively expands the candidate set: at each hop rr, it retrieves the top-κr\kappa_{r} predecessors of the tokens reached at the previous hop, allowing access to tokens up to mm hops away. Each subsequent sparse layer computes new queries from the current token representations and attends to these candidates using the original full-attention keys and values. The candidate sets are computed once and remain fixed throughout the block, allowing the sparse layers to refine their queries without recomputing retrieval routes. By enabling retrieved tokens to guide further retrievals, MuRA supports complex chains of dependent retrievals while preserving the efficiency of existing hybrid designs: for fixed retrieval parameters, sparse retrieval layers require linear computation in sequence length and maintain constant-size states, introducing no additional KV caches.

Theoretically, we prove that for any fixed mm, a single mm-hop MuRA block can compute compositions of mm functions with constant width and depth and only logarithmic precision. To our knowledge, this provides the first architecture with a single full-attention layer that is provably capable of such multi-step function composition. We further establish the importance of retrieval depth, showing that computing compositions of m+1m+1 functions with at most mm retrieval hops requires size Ω⁡(n1/(m+1))\Omega(n^{1/(m+1)}). Together, these results establish a strict hierarchy in expressive power as retrieval depth increases. This separation holds even when the total number of retrieved KV entries is matched, demonstrating that the structure of retrieval, rather than merely the number of retrieved tokens, is critical to expressivity.

Empirically, we evaluate MuRA on synthetic function-composition tasks to investigate whether its theoretical advantages can also be realized through training. For m∈{1,2,3,4}m\in\{1,2,3,4\}, we find that models with a single mm-hop MuRA block achieve near-perfect test accuracy on compositions of up to mm functions, while struggling with deeper compositions. In contrast, the existing hybrid architectures we evaluate struggle with compositions involving more than one function. These results demonstrate that the expressive advantages of MuRA can be learned in practice on controlled tasks, supporting multi-hop retrieval as a promising design principle for more expressive hybrid architectures.

In summary, our main contributions are:

  • •

    Expressivity limitations of existing hybrid architectures. We establish an Ω⁡(n)\Omega(\sqrt{n}) size lower bound for single-block hybrid architectures on function composition tasks, covering both conventional blocks, and those whose layers access a shared KV cache through top-κ\kappa retrieval.

  • •

    Multi-Hop Retrieval Attention. We introduce MuRA, which enables recurrent layers to perform multi-hop retrieval from a shared KV cache while preserving the computational and memory efficiency of existing hybrid architectures.

  • •

    Expressivity improvements. We prove that a single mm-hop MuRA block can compute compositions of mm functions with constant width and depth and logarithmic precision, and establish a strict expressivity hierarchy in retrieval depth, even under matched retrieval budgets.

  • •

    Empirical validation. We demonstrate that this hierarchy emerges through training on synthetic function-composition tasks with up to four retrieval hops, substantially outperforming existing hybrid baselines.

2 Hybrid Blocks: Existing Architectures and Expressivity Limitations

We begin this section by defining the three main components of hybrid blocks: full-attention layers, recurrent layers, and top-κ\kappa access recurrent layers. We then introduce a unified framework capturing commonly used hybrid architectures, as well as recent designs that allow recurrent layers to access the full-attention KV cache. Finally, we establish lower bounds on the size of hybrid blocks required to solve function composition, a well-studied task in sequence-model expressivity [33; 47] involving successive dependent retrievals, as often arise in multi-hop reasoning.

2.1 Hybrid Block Components and Structure

We first formalize the three classes of layers used to construct hybrid blocks. Throughout, bold lowercase and uppercase letters denote vectors and matrices, respectively (e.g., 𝒗{\bm{v}} and 𝑿{\bm{X}}), and [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}.

Definition 2.1.

A multi-head attention layer 𝖠\mathsf{A} of width dd consists of hh attention heads, each of dimension d/hd/h. Given an input sequence 𝑿=[𝒙1,…,𝒙N]⊤∈ℝN×d{\bm{X}}=[{\bm{x}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{N}]^{\top}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N\times d}, each head j∈[h]j\in[h] computes queries 𝑸j=𝑿​𝑾Q,j{\bm{Q}}_{j}={\bm{X}}{\bm{W}}_{Q,j}, keys 𝑲j=𝑿​𝑾K,j{\bm{K}}_{j}={\bm{X}}{\bm{W}}_{K,j}, and values 𝑽j=𝑿​𝑾V,j{\bm{V}}_{j}={\bm{X}}{\bm{W}}_{V,j}, using learned projections 𝑾Q,j,𝑾K,j,𝑾V,j∈ℝd×(d/h){\bm{W}}_{Q,j},{\bm{W}}_{K,j},{\bm{W}}_{V,j}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d\times(d/h)}. The layer computes

headj​(𝑿)\displaystyle\mathrm{head}_{j}({\bm{X}}) =softmax⁡(𝑸j​𝑲j⊤d/h+𝑴)​𝑽j,\displaystyle=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{{\bm{Q}}_{j}{\bm{K}}_{j}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d/h}}+{\bm{M}}\right){\bm{V}}_{j}, (1)
𝖠⁡(𝑿)\displaystyle\mathsf{A}({\bm{X}}) =𝑿+[headj​(𝑿)]j=1h​𝑾O.\displaystyle={\bm{X}}+[\mathrm{head}_{j}({\bm{X}})]_{j=1}^{h}{\bm{W}}_{O}.

Here, 𝑾O∈ℝd×d{\bm{W}}_{O}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d\times d} is a learned output projection, the softmax is applied row-wise, and the causal mask 𝑴∈ℝN×N{\bm{M}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N\times N} satisfies 𝑴i,t=0{\bm{M}}_{i,t}=0 for t≤it\leq i and 𝑴i,t=−∞{\bm{M}}_{i,t}=-\infty otherwise. For each head jj, we define the attention score αi,t(j)\alpha_{i,t}^{(j)} from token ii to token tt as the (i,t)(i,t) entry of the softmax matrix above.

For a fixed layer width, full attention processes a sequence of length NN in O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) time, computing pairwise query–key similarities and aggregating the corresponding values. During autoregressive inference, the keys and values of preceding tokens remain unchanged and are therefore stored in a KV cache, avoiding their recomputation when processing new tokens. This requires O⁡(N)O(N) memory per layer, and reduces the computational complexity for each new token to O⁡(N)O(N). These costs motivate using full-attention layers sparingly and interleaving them with more efficient recurrent layers, which we define next.

Definition 2.2.

A recurrent layer 𝖱\mathsf{R} of width dd is specified by a fixed initial state 𝒉0∈ℝd{\bm{h}}_{0}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} and two functions f,g:ℝd×ℝd→ℝdf,g:{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, representing the state transition and output maps, respectively. Given an input sequence 𝑿=[𝒙1,…,𝒙N]⊤∈ℝN×d{\bm{X}}=[{\bm{x}}_{1},\dots,{\bm{x}}_{N}]^{\top}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N\times d}, the layer computes

𝒉i=f⁡(𝒉i−1,𝒙i),𝒚i=g⁡(𝒉i,𝒙i),{\bm{h}}_{i}=f({\bm{h}}_{i-1},{\bm{x}}_{i}),\qquad{\bm{y}}_{i}=g({\bm{h}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{i}), (2)

and outputs 𝖱⁡(𝑿)=[𝒚1,…,𝒚N]⊤\mathsf{R}({\bm{X}})=[{\bm{y}}_{1},\dots,{\bm{y}}_{N}]^{\top}.

We leave the parameterization of ff and gg unrestricted to encompass a range of widely used recurrent architectures [19; 18; 46]. Our framework also captures efficient attention variants, including sliding-window attention [2] and kernel-based linear attention [21]. See appendix A for further details.

For fixed layer width, recurrent layers process a sequence of length NN in O⁡(N)O(N) time. Additionally, during autoregressive inference, each new token at position tt is processed using only the preceding state 𝒉t−1{\bm{h}}_{t-1}, requiring constant memory and computation per token. While this makes recurrent layers significantly more efficient than full attention, their bounded memory can limit long-context performance [42; 35], motivating hybrid architectures that combine recurrent and full-attention layers.

Since full attention maintains a richer memory in the form of a growing KV cache, recent approaches [13; 43] seek to exploit this resource by allowing recurrent layers to access a fixed number of the highest-scoring KV entries per token, aiming to improve performance while preserving efficiency. This motivates the following definition.

Definition 2.3.

Fix κ∈ℕ\kappa\in{\mathbb{N}} and a full-attention layer 𝖠\mathsf{A} of width dd with hh heads. For each head j∈[h]j\in[h], let 𝑲j=[𝒌1j,…,𝒌Nj]⊤{\bm{K}}^{j}=[{\bm{k}}_{1}^{j},\dots,{\bm{k}}_{N}^{j}]^{\top} and 𝑽j=[𝒗1j,…,𝒗Nj]⊤{\bm{V}}^{j}=[{\bm{v}}_{1}^{j},\dots,{\bm{v}}_{N}^{j}]^{\top}, both in ℝN×(d/h){\mathbb{R}}^{N\times(d/h)}, denote its cached keys and values. For each position i∈[N]i\in[N] and head j∈[h]j\in[h], let 𝒩j(κ)​(i)\mathcal{N}_{j}^{(\kappa)}(i) consist of position ii and the min⁡{κ,i−1}\min\{\kappa,i-1\} preceding positions with the highest attention scores αi,t(j)\alpha_{i,t}^{(j)}, breaking ties in favor of more recent positions. The corresponding retrieved KV entries are

𝑪i=[[𝒌tj,𝒗tj]t∈𝒩j(κ)​(i)]j=1h.{\bm{C}}_{i}=\Bigl[\bigl[{\bm{k}}_{t}^{j},{\bm{v}}_{t}^{j}\bigr]_{t\in\mathcal{N}_{j}^{(\kappa)}(i)}\Bigr]_{j=1}^{h}. (3)

A top-κ\kappa access recurrent layer 𝖱κ\mathsf{R}_{\kappa} of width dd is defined by a fixed initial state 𝒉0∈ℝd{\bm{h}}_{0}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} and two functions ff and gg, specifying the state transition and output, respectively. Given an input sequence 𝑿=[𝒙1,…,𝒙N]⊤∈ℝN×d{\bm{X}}=[{\bm{x}}_{1},\dots,{\bm{x}}_{N}]^{\top}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N\times d}, the layer computes

𝒉i=f⁡(𝒉i−1,𝒙i,𝑪i),𝒚i=g⁡(𝒉i,𝒙i,𝑪i),{\bm{h}}_{i}=f({\bm{h}}_{i-1},{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{C}}_{i}),\qquad{\bm{y}}_{i}=g({\bm{h}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{C}}_{i}), (4)

and outputs 𝖱κ​(𝑿)=[𝒚1,…,𝒚N]⊤\mathsf{R}_{\kappa}({\bm{X}})=[{\bm{y}}_{1},\dots,{\bm{y}}_{N}]^{\top}.

Compared with standard recurrent layers, top-κ\kappa access recurrent layers incur additional computation only for computing the neighborhoods 𝒩j(κ)​(i)\mathcal{N}_{j}^{(\kappa)}(i) and retrieving the corresponding KV entries 𝑪i{\bm{C}}_{i}. As demonstrated by Gao et al. [13], attention-based neighborhood selection can be performed without increasing the asymptotic complexity of full attention, and can be implemented efficiently in practice using algorithms such as FlashAttention[8]. For fixed κ\kappa and layer width, retrieving 𝑪i{\bm{C}}_{i} requires constant time per token. Furthermore, both operations need only be performed once per full-attention layer, and their results can be shared across multiple subsequent recurrent layers. Having defined these three classes of layers, we now formalize the hybrid blocks considered in this work.

Definition 2.4.

For nonnegative integers κ\kappa, LpreL_{\mathrm{pre}} and LpostL_{\mathrm{post}}, a top-κ\kappa access hybrid block 𝖡κ\mathsf{B}_{\kappa} of width dd consists of LpreL_{\mathrm{pre}} standard recurrent layers 𝖱1pre,…,𝖱Lprepre\mathsf{R}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{1},\dots,\mathsf{R}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{L_{\mathrm{pre}}}, a causal full-attention layer 𝖠\mathsf{A}, and LpostL_{\mathrm{post}} top-κ\kappa access recurrent layers 𝖱1post,…,𝖱Lpostpost\mathsf{R}^{\mathrm{post}}_{1},\dots,\mathsf{R}^{\mathrm{post}}_{L_{\mathrm{post}}} . All post-attention layers have access to layer 𝖠\mathsf{A}’ KV cache. For an input sequence 𝑿∈ℝN×d{\bm{X}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N\times d}, the block computes

𝖡κ(𝑿)=(𝖱Lpostpost∘⋯∘𝖱1post∘𝖠∘𝖱Lprepre∘⋯∘𝖱1pre)(𝑿).\mathsf{B}_{\kappa}({\bm{X}})=\bigl(\mathsf{R}^{\mathrm{post}}_{L_{\mathrm{post}}}\circ\cdots\circ\mathsf{R}^{\mathrm{post}}_{1}\circ\mathsf{A}\circ\mathsf{R}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{L_{\mathrm{pre}}}\circ\cdots\circ\mathsf{R}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{1}\bigr)({\bm{X}}). (5)

Definition 2.4 captures several prominent hybrid block designs.11 1 In practice, hybrid models usually use attention layers as part of transformer blocks, typically including layer normalization and position-wise feed-forward networks. We omit these token-wise operations from our theoretical analysis, as they can be incorporated into adjacent recurrent layers without affecting our results, but retain them in our experiments; see Appendix A. In particular, top-00 access blocks represent conventional hybrid architectures, such as those used by Kimi K3 [40], Gemma 3 [16], Nemotron 3 Ultra [3], and OLMo Hybrid [27], while top-κ\kappa access blocks capture the more recent shared-KV mechanisms introduced by HySparse [13] and HySparse2 [43].

Top-κ\kappa access offers one approach to reusing the existing KV cache within efficient layers. We next investigate whether such shared-memory access can enhance the expressivity of hybrid blocks, and whether top-κ\kappa retrieval is sufficient to realize these benefits. Studying expressivity at the block level is particularly relevant for designing efficient hybrid models: increasing the capabilities of individual blocks through relatively inexpensive sequence layers could reduce the number of full-attention layers required, thereby saving computation and KV-cache memory.

2.2 Expressivity Limitations of Hybrid Blocks on Function Composition.

Below, we establish expressivity limitations for individual top-κ\kappa access hybrid blocks. We treat each block as a sequence model, embedding input tokens into vectors of width dd and applying an unembedding layer to the final token representation to produce the output (see Appendix A for details). Throughout, we assume pp bits of precision per scalar, where pp may scale with the sequence length NN. Our analysis focuses on function composition, a standard task in sequence-model expressivity analysis [33; 22; 6; 47].

Definition 2.5.

Given integers m,n∈ℕm,n\in{\mathbb{N}}, functions f1,…,fm:[n]→[n]f_{1},\ldots,f_{m}:[n]\to[n] and a query x∈[n]x\in[n], we construct a sequence of length N=m​n+1N=mn+1 over the alphabet [n][n] by concatenating the function tables and appending the query:

𝒂⁡(f1,…,fm,x)=(CLOSE\displaystyle{\bm{a}}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{m},x)=\bigl( OPENf1​(1),…,f1​(n),…,fm​(1),…,fm​(n),x).\displaystyle f_{1}(1),\ldots,f_{1}(n),\ldots,f_{m}(1),\ldots,f_{m}(n),x\bigr). (6)

The mm-function composition task requires a sequence model to output, at the final position,

Fm,n(𝒂(f1,…,fm,x))=(f1∘⋯∘fm)(x).F_{m,n}({\bm{a}}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{m},x))=(f_{1}\circ\cdots\circ f_{m})(x). (7)

Function composition captures a fundamental aspect of multi-hop reasoning, in which solving a problem requires multiple dependent retrievals. For example, answering a question about the birthplace of a person’s father requires first identifying the father and then retrieving his birthplace. To analyze the ability of hybrid blocks to perform such computations, we establish a connection between their expressive power and one-way multiparty number-on-the-forehead (NOF) communication protocols [41], defined below.

Definition 2.6.

For m,n∈ℕm,n\in{\mathbb{N}}, a one-way (m+1)(m+1)-player number-on-the-forehead (NOF) communication protocol consists of m+1m+1 players P1,…,Pm+1P_{1},\ldots,P_{m+1} with a fixed communication procedure. Given input functions f1,…,fm:[n]→[n]f_{1},\ldots,f_{m}:[n]\to[n] and a query x∈[n]x\in[n], each player PjP_{j}, for j∈[m]j\in[m], has access to xx and all functions except fjf_{j}, while player Pm+1P_{m+1} has access to all functions but not xx.

Communication proceeds in the fixed order Pm+1→Pm→⋯→P1P_{m+1}\to P_{m}\to\cdots\to P_{1}. Each player except P1P_{1} sends a single message, determined by its available inputs and all preceding messages according to the fixed protocol. Finally, P1P_{1} produces an output based on its available information and the received messages. The communication cost is the maximum, over all possible inputs, of the sum of the bit lengths of all transmitted messages.

A classical result in communication complexity [41] establishes that any one-way (m+1)(m+1)-player NOF protocol computing mm-function composition for all possible inputs requires Ω⁡(n1/m)\Omega(n^{1/m}) bits of communication. We use this lower bound throughout our analysis, beginning with its three-player case (m=2m=2) to establish a capacity lower bound for top-κ\kappa access hybrid blocks.

Theorem 2.7.

Let 𝖡κ\mathsf{B}_{\kappa} be a top-κ\kappa access hybrid block with LpreL_{\mathrm{pre}} pre-attention layers and LpostL_{\mathrm{post}} post-attention layers, width dd, and precision pp. Define its capacity as

C⁡(𝖡κ)=p​d​(Lpost+κ+1).C(\mathsf{B}_{\kappa})=pd(L_{\mathrm{post}}+\kappa+1). (8)

If for some integer m≥2m\geq 2, 𝖡κ\mathsf{B}_{\kappa} computes mm-function composition for all sequences encoding functions f1,…,fm:[n]→[n]f_{1},\ldots,f_{m}:[n]\to[n] and queries x∈[n]x\in[n], then

C⁡(𝖡κ)=Ω⁡(n).C(\mathsf{B}_{\kappa})=\Omega(\sqrt{n}). (9)

We outline the main argument below, with the full proof provided in Appendix B.1.

Proof sketch.

We show that any top-κ\kappa access hybrid block 𝖡κ\mathsf{B}_{\kappa} computing mm-function composition induces a three-player NOF protocol for two-function composition with communication cost O⁡(C⁡(𝖡κ))O(C(\mathsf{B}_{\kappa})). For m>2m>2, we fix f3,…,fmf_{3},\ldots,f_{m} to be the identity. Given inputs f1,f2,xf_{1},f_{2},x, the players jointly simulate the block’s forward pass on the corresponding sequence of length N=m​n+1N=mn+1.

Player P3P_{3} (knows f1,f2f_{1},f_{2}): Since all tokens preceding the final query xx are known to P3P_{3}, it can compute their representations and recurrent states throughout the block. It transmits the states of the last pre-attention recurrent layer at positions nn and N−1N-1, together with the states of all post-attention layers at position nn. Player P2P_{2} (knows f1,xf_{1},x): Using the received pre attention state at position N−1N-1, P2P_{2} can reconstruct the last token’s attention query, as well as all keys and values corresponding to the first function table. For each attention head, it computes the contribution of these tokens to the attention output, represented by an unnormalized weighted sum and its softmax normalization factor. It also computes the top-κ\kappa highest-scoring KV entries within the first nn tokens along with their attention scores. These quantities are transmitted to P1P_{1}. Player P1P_{1} (knows f2,xf_{2},x): Using the recurrent states received from P3P_{3}, player P1P_{1} reconstructs the representations of tokens n+1,…,Nn+1,\dots,N, and computes their contribution to the final attention output. Combining this with the quantities received from P2P_{2}, it recovers the full-attention output and the globally selected top-κ\kappa KV entries. Finally, using the post-attention recurrent states provided by P3P_{3}, it completes the forward pass and outputs f1​(f2​(x))f_{1}(f_{2}(x)).

The total communication cost of the protocol above is O⁡(C⁡(𝖡κ))O(C(\mathsf{B}_{\kappa})). The classical three-player NOF lower bound therefore implies C⁡(𝖡κ)=Ω⁡(n)C(\mathsf{B}_{\kappa})=\Omega(\sqrt{n}). ∎

Remark.

Ye et al. [47] also establish polynomial lower bounds for hybrid architectures, including those with multiple full-attention layers. However, specializing their result to hybrid blocks using a single full-attention layer yields an N1/1024N^{1/1024} lower bound on model capacity and assumes a bound on the number of efficient sequence layers. In contrast, we establish an Ω⁡(n)\Omega(\sqrt{n}) capacity lower bound that allows arbitrary recurrent depth and also extends to top-κ\kappa memory access.

3 Multi-Hop Retrieval from Shared Attention Memory

Theorem 2.7 reveals a fundamental limitation of top-κ\kappa access hybrid blocks in performing multi-hop reasoning. To address this limitation, we introduce Multi-hop Retrieval Attention (MuRA), a new hybrid block architecture that allows sparse-attention layers to access the existing KV cache through multiple retrieval hops. We first formally define (κ1,…,κm)(\kappa_{1},\ldots,\kappa_{m})-MuRA blocks and then establish their expressive advantage over existing hybrid architectures on function composition. In particular, we show that retrieval depth induces a strict expressivity hierarchy: an mm-hop block can compute mm-function composition with constant width and logarithmic capacity, whereas computing (m+1)(m+1)-function composition requires polynomial capacity. Importantly, these expressive gains come without increasing the asymptotic computational or memory complexity of existing hybrid blocks.

3.1 MuRA Hybrid Blocks

To overcome the multi-hop expressivity limitations of top-κ\kappa access hybrid blocks, we propose a simple extension to the set of KV entries available to subsequent layers. Rather than retrieving only the tokens with the highest attention scores relative to the current position, we also retrieve tokens that are highly attended to by those already selected, recursively expanding the retrieved set over multiple hops.

For a fixed full-attention layer 𝖠\mathsf{A}, recall that 𝒩j(κ)​(i)\mathcal{N}_{j}^{(\kappa)}(i) denotes the top-κ\kappa neighborhood of position ii for attention head jj (Definition 2.3). Given retrieval widths κ1,…,κm∈ℕ\kappa_{1},\ldots,\kappa_{m}\in{\mathbb{N}}, we recursively define multi-hop neighborhood 𝒩j(κ1,…,κr)​(i)\mathcal{N}_{j}^{(\kappa_{1},\ldots,\kappa_{r})}(i) by

𝒩j(κ1,…,κr)​(i)=⋃t∈𝒩j(κ1,…,κr−1)​(i)𝒩j(κr)​(t),2≤r≤m.\mathcal{N}_{j}^{(\kappa_{1},\ldots,\kappa_{r})}(i)=\bigcup_{t\in\mathcal{N}_{j}^{(\kappa_{1},\ldots,\kappa_{r-1})}(i)}\mathcal{N}_{j}^{(\kappa_{r})}(t),\qquad 2\leq r\leq m. (10)

The resulting neighborhoods contain chains of tokens connected by high-scoring attention links,22 2 Since the one-hop neighborhoods 𝒩j(κ)​(i)\mathcal{N}_{j}^{(\kappa)}(i) include position ii itself, mm-hop neighborhoods contains all positions reachable within at most mm hops. In practice, we also consider a variant that restricts retrieval to positions reachable in exactly mm hops. We find this variant is sometimes preferable empirically, while retaining the original convention for our theoretical analysis. potentially exposing information that cannot be accessed by top-κ\kappa retrieval. We now define MuRA sparse-attention layers, which attend only to retrieved multi-hop positions.

Definition 3.1.

Fix 𝜿=(κ1,…,κm)∈ℕm\bm{\kappa}=(\kappa_{1},\dots,\kappa_{m})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{m} and full-attention layer 𝖠\mathsf{A} of width dd with hh heads. For each head j∈[h]j\in[h], denote its cached keys and values by 𝑲j=[𝒌1j,…,𝒌Nj]⊤{\bm{K}}^{j}=[{\bm{k}}_{1}^{j},\dots,{\bm{k}}_{N}^{j}]^{\top} and 𝑽j=[𝒗1j,…,𝒗Nj]⊤{\bm{V}}^{j}=[{\bm{v}}_{1}^{j},\dots,{\bm{v}}_{N}^{j}]^{\top}, both in ℝN×(d/h){\mathbb{R}}^{N\times(d/h)}. A 𝜿\bm{\kappa}-MuRA multi-head attention layer 𝖲\mathsf{S} is specified by hh query projection heads 𝑾Q,j∈ℝd×(d/h){\bm{W}}_{Q,j}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d\times(d/h)} and hh integer tuples 𝜿j=(κ1j,…,κmj1)\bm{\kappa}_{j}=(\kappa_{1}^{j},\dots,\kappa^{1}_{m_{j}}) with mj≤mm_{j}\leq m and κij≤κi∀i∈[mj]\kappa^{j}_{i}\leq\kappa_{i}\quad\forall i\in[m_{j}]. Given an input sequence 𝑿=[𝒙1,…,𝒙N]⊤∈ℝN×d{\bm{X}}=[{\bm{x}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{N}]^{\top}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N\times d}, each head j∈[h]j\in[h] computes queries 𝑸j=𝑿​𝑾Q,j{\bm{Q}}_{j}={\bm{X}}{\bm{W}}_{Q,j} and reuses the full attention keys and values, to compute

headj​(𝑿)\displaystyle\mathrm{head}_{j}({\bm{X}}) =softmax⁡(𝑸j​𝑲j⊤d/h+𝑴𝜿j)​𝑽j,\displaystyle=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{{\bm{Q}}_{j}{\bm{K}}_{j}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d/h}}+{\bm{M}}_{\bm{\kappa}_{j}}\right){\bm{V}}_{j}, (11)
𝖠⁡(𝑿)\displaystyle\mathsf{A}({\bm{X}}) =𝑿+[headj​(𝑿)]j=1h​𝑾O.\displaystyle={\bm{X}}+[\mathrm{head}_{j}({\bm{X}})]_{j=1}^{h}{\bm{W}}_{O}.

Here, 𝑾O∈ℝd×d{\bm{W}}_{O}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d\times d} is a learned output projection, the softmax is applied row-wise, and the mask 𝑴𝜿j∈ℝN×N{\bm{M}}_{\bm{\kappa}_{j}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N\times N} satisfies 𝑴i,t=0{\bm{M}}_{i,t}=0 for t∈𝒩j𝜿j​(i)t\in\mathcal{N}_{j}^{\bm{\kappa}_{j}}(i) and 𝑴i,t=−∞{\bm{M}}_{i,t}=-\infty otherwise. We refer to mm as the retrieval depth of 𝖲\mathsf{S}.

Importantly, MuRA preserves the asymptotic efficiency of top-κ\kappa access layers. For fixed retrieval depths and widths 𝜿\bm{\kappa}, each neighborhood 𝒩j𝜿j​(i)\mathcal{N}_{j}^{\bm{\kappa}_{j}}(i) contains a constant number of positions independent of the sequence length NN. Consequently, each sparse-attention layer attends to only a fixed number of KV entries per token, retaining the same asymptotic computational and memory complexity as top-κ\kappa access. Although the neighborhood size can grow exponentially with retrieval depth mm, we show later that even the minimal choice κ1=⋯=κm=1\kappa_{1}=\cdots=\kappa_{m}=1 is sufficient to improve expressive power, and that higher retrieval depth increases expressivity even for a matched number of retrieved tokens.

Beyond these theoretical guarantees, MuRA also admits a practical implementation strategy. HySparse [13] demonstrates that attention-based routing information can be extracted alongside full attention using a modified FlashAttention kernel, without materializing the full attention matrix, and employs this approach to train 7B language models. Building on this design, multi-hop retrieval requires only an additional traversal of the selected token indices to construct the expanded neighborhoods, which can then be shared across all subsequent sparse-attention layers. The underlying KV cache and full-attention computation remain unchanged, making MuRA a natural extension of existing efficient implementations. We now formally define MuRA hybrid blocks.

Definition 3.2.

For nonnegative integers LpreL_{\mathrm{pre}} and LpostL_{\mathrm{post}}, and 𝜿∈ℕm\bm{\kappa}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{m} a 𝛋\bm{\kappa}-MuRA hybrid block 𝖡𝜿\mathsf{B}_{\bm{\kappa}} of width dd consists of LpreL_{\mathrm{pre}} standard recurrent layers 𝖱1pre,…,𝖱Lprepre\mathsf{R}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{1},\dots,\mathsf{R}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{L_{\mathrm{pre}}}, a causal full-attention layer 𝖠\mathsf{A}, and LpostL_{\mathrm{post}} 𝜿\bm{\kappa}-MuRA attention layers 𝖲1post,…,𝖲Lpostpost\mathsf{S}^{\mathrm{post}}_{1},\dots,\mathsf{S}^{\mathrm{post}}_{L_{\mathrm{post}}}. All post-attention layers have access to the KV cache of layer 𝖠\mathsf{A}. For an input sequence 𝑿∈ℝN×d{\bm{X}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N\times d}, the block computes

𝖡𝜿(𝑿)=(𝖲Lpostpost∘⋯∘𝖲1post∘𝖠∘𝖱Lprepre∘⋯∘𝖱1pre)(𝑿).\mathsf{B}_{\bm{\kappa}}({\bm{X}})=\bigl(\mathsf{S}^{\mathrm{post}}_{L_{\mathrm{post}}}\circ\cdots\circ\mathsf{S}^{\mathrm{post}}_{1}\circ\mathsf{A}\circ\mathsf{R}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{L_{\mathrm{pre}}}\circ\cdots\circ\mathsf{R}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{1}\bigr)({\bm{X}}). (12)

3.2 The Expressive Power of MuRA Hybrid Blocks.

We study the effects of retrieval depth on the expressive power of MuRA hybrid blocks. Our first result shows that even the minimal choice of retrieving a single predecessor per hop is sufficient to efficiently compute function composition, with the number of hops matching the number of composed functions. The full proof appears in Appendix B.2, and illustrated in Figure 1.

Theorem 3.3.

For every fixed m≥1m\geq 1, a single (1,…,1⏞m)(\overbrace{1,\ldots,1}^{m})-MuRA block can compute mm-function composition for every n≥2n\geq 2 using a single attention head, a single MuRA sparse attention layer, no recurrent layers, width d=O⁡(m)d=O(m) independent of the sequence length NN, and precision p=O⁡(l​o​g​(N))p=O(log(N)).

Proof sketch.

Consider an input sequence 𝒂⁡(f1,…,fm,x){\bm{a}}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{m},x) as in Definition 2.5. We embed each token corresponding to fi​(j)f_{i}(j) via a function of its table index i∈[m]i\in[m], input argument j∈[n]j\in[n], and value fi​(j)∈[n]f_{i}(j)\in[n].33 3 While this encoding differs from standard positional embeddings, it can be recovered from them using a single pre-attention recurrent layer. See Appendix A for details. We can then construct a full-attention layer 𝖠\mathsf{A} such that, for every i>1i>1, the unique top-11 predecessor of the token representing fi​(j)f_{i}(j) is the token representing fi−1​(fi​(j))f_{i-1}(f_{i}(j)). Similarly, the top-11 predecessor of the final query token xx is the token representing fm​(x)f_{m}(x). Consequently, the mm-hop neighborhood 𝒩(1,…,1)​(x)\mathcal{N}^{(1,\ldots,1)}(x) contains precisely the tokens along the composition chain

x→fm(x)→(fm−1∘fm)(x)→⋯→(f1∘⋯∘fm)(x).x\to f_{m}(x)\to(f_{m-1}\circ f_{m})(x)\to\cdots\to(f_{1}\circ\cdots\circ f_{m})(x). (13)

We set the full-attention output projection 𝑾O{\bm{W}}_{O} to zero, preserving the input representations through the residual connection. A single sparse-attention layer then attends to the retrieved composition chain. Since only the final token in the retrieved chain belongs to the first function table, we choose the full-attention value projection so that the last coordinate of each cached value contains the function value for tokens from the first table and zero otherwise. Setting the sparse-attention query to zero induces uniform attention over the m+1m+1 retrieved tokens, yielding 1m+1(f1∘⋯∘fm)(x)\frac{1}{m+1}(f_{1}\circ\cdots\circ f_{m})(x) in the last output coordinate. Rescaling by m+1m+1 recovers the desired composition, completing the construction. ∎

We next establish a strict expressivity hierarchy in retrieval depth: each additional hop enables higher-order function composition with logarithmic capacity, while blocks with fewer hops require polynomial capacity, regardless of the number of (fixed) retrieved KV entries. This highlights the importance of retrieval depth over retrieval size. The full proof appears in Appendix B.3.

Theorem 3.4.

For 𝛋∈ℕm\bm{\kappa}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{m}, with m≥2m\geq 2, let 𝖡𝛋\mathsf{B}_{\bm{\kappa}} be a 𝛋\bm{\kappa}-MuRA model with 𝛋=(κ1,…,κm)\bm{\kappa}=(\kappa_{1},\dots,\kappa_{m}), LpreL_{\mathrm{pre}} pre-attention layers and LpostL_{\mathrm{post}} post-attention layers, width dd, and precision pp. Define its capacity as

C⁡(𝖡κ)=p​d​m⋅Πi=1m​κi.C(\mathsf{B}_{\kappa})=pdm\cdot\Pi_{i=1}^{m}\kappa_{i}. (14)

If 𝖡𝛋\mathsf{B}_{\bm{\kappa}} computes (m+1)(m+1)-function composition on every instance of size nn, then

C⁡(𝖡𝜿)=Ω⁡(n1/(m+1)).C(\mathsf{B}_{\bm{\kappa}})=\Omega(n^{1/(m+1)}).
Proof sketch.

We extend the reduction of Theorem 2.7 to an (m+2)(m+2)-player NOF protocol for (m+1)(m+1)-function composition. Given a 𝜿\bm{\kappa}-MuRA block, the players simulate its forward pass on sequences 𝒂⁡(f1,…,fm+1,x){\bm{a}}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{m+1},x) of length N=(m+1)​n+1N=(m+1)n+1. Player Pm+2P_{m+2} knows all function tables but not the query xx, while each PiP_{i}, for i∈[m+1]i\in[m+1], knows xx and all function tables except fif_{i}.

Full attention computation: Since Pm+2P_{m+2} knows all tokens preceding xx, it can compute their representations and transmit the recurrent states needed at the boundaries between function tables. As in the previous proof, Pm+1P_{m+1} computes the contribution of the first mm function tables to the final token’s attention output, represented by an unnormalized weighted sum and its softmax normalization factor. Player PmP_{m} then adds the contribution of the remaining tokens corresponding to function m+1m+1, recovering the full-attention output.

Retrieval: The players simulate the mm retrieval hops sequentially, starting with Pm+1P_{m+1}. At each stage, player PiP_{i} computes attention scores with respect to the previously retrieved tokens and selects the top-κm+2−i\kappa_{m+2-i} candidates among all tokens, except those corresponding to fif_{i}, the only function table it cannot access. It transmits these candidates and their attention scores to Pi−1P_{i-1}, which knows fif_{i} and can therefore complete the global top-κm+2−i\kappa_{m+2-i} selection. Using the transmitted recurrent states, Pi−1P_{i-1} continues the computation and prepares the candidates for the next hop. In this way, each successive player completes one additional retrieval hop. Since the block performs only mm hops, player P1P_{1} can recover the final retrieved KV entries, complete the forward pass, and output (f1∘⋯∘fm+1)(x)(f_{1}\circ\cdots\circ f_{m+1})(x).

The resulting protocol has communication cost O⁡(C⁡(𝖡))O(C(\mathsf{B})). Applying the (m+2)(m+2)-player NOF pointer-jumping lower bound yields C⁡(𝖡)=Ω⁡(n1/(m+1))C(\mathsf{B})=\Omega(n^{1/(m+1)}), as claimed.

∎

4 Empirical Evaluation

We empirically validate our theoretical findings on a synthetic function-composition benchmark. Our results show that existing hybrid architectures struggle to learn compositions, whereas MuRA successfully learns increasingly complex compositions as retrieval depth grows, demonstrating the benefits of multi-hop access to the shared KV cache. We provide the main experimental details and results below, with a more comprehensive description in Appendix C.

Synthetic benchmark.

We construct a synthetic dataset of 250,000 sequences, each encoding five functions f1,…,f5:[n]→[n]f_{1},\ldots,f_{5}:[n]\to[n], where n∈{25,…,30}n\in\{25,\ldots,30\} and all function values are sampled independently and uniformly from [n][n]. The function tables are serialized as in Definition 2.5, omitting the final query token. We train hybrid blocks on a causal token-prediction task that jointly evaluates function composition at depths m∈[4]m\in[4]. Specifically, each token representing fi​(j)f_{i}(j) is assigned multiple composition targets by treating its value as the query x=fi​(j)x=f_{i}(j) and applying the preceding functions:

fi−1(fi(j)),(fi−2∘fi−1)(fi(j)),…,(f1∘⋯∘fi−1)(fi(j)).f_{i-1}(f_{i}(j)),\;(f_{i-2}\circ f_{i-1})(f_{i}(j)),\;\ldots,\;(f_{1}\circ\cdots\circ f_{i-1})(f_{i}(j)). (15)

These targets are predicted from each token’s final representation. We evaluate accuracy at each composition depth m∈[4]m\in[4] over all tokens for which the corresponding composition is defined. Models are trained for 500 epochs using cross-entropy loss over all composition targets. The dataset is split into 200,000 training, 25,000 validation, and 25,000 test examples, and we report test accuracy at the checkpoint selected by the best validation score.

Baselines and architecture details.

All experiments use a single hybrid block comprising of one full-attention layer followed by four efficient sequence layers, each with four heads and hidden dimension d=16d=16. All models use the same positional encoding, supervision, and optimizer. We evaluate 𝜿\bm{\kappa}-MuRA with 𝜿∈{(32),(16,1),(11,1,1),(8,1,1,1)}\bm{\kappa}\in\{(32),(16,1),(11,1,1),(8,1,1,1)\}, corresponding to retrieval depths of one through four hops. These configurations are chosen to have approximately the same retrieval budget of 32 tokens (33 for (11,1,1)(11,1,1)). The single-hop configuration (32)(32) corresponds to a simplified version of HySparse [13]. To facilitate learning at different composition depths, each head jj of a MuRA sparse-attention layer uses a retrieval tuple 𝜿j=(κ1,…,κmin⁡(j,m))\bm{\kappa}_{j}=(\kappa_{1},\ldots,\kappa_{\min(j,m)}), allowing earlier heads to access only shallower retrieval neighborhoods. We compare MuRA against Gated DeltaNet [46], linear attention [21], and sliding-window attention [2]. For sliding-window attention, we evaluate window sizes of both 32 and 16 tokens. While a window of 32 matches the retrieval budget of MuRA, each sliding-window layer maintains its own KV cache, resulting in a combined cache size comparable to an additional full-attention layer in our setting. We therefore also consider a window size of 16 to provide a more memory-efficient baseline.

Discussion.

Table 1 demonstrates a clear relationship between retrieval depth and the ability to learn function composition. MuRA blocks achieve near-perfect accuracy on mm-function composition when their retrieval depth is at least mm, while shallower configurations fail to fully learn the task. Interestingly, shallower configurations sometimes achieve accuracy substantially above random guessing, but remain far from perfect and exhibit considerably higher variance across seeds. Consistent with our theoretical findings, the baseline hybrid blocks generally perform well on single-function composition but fail on deeper compositions. Even sliding-window attention with a window size of 32, which requires additional KV caches comparable in total size to another full-attention layer, struggles on more complex function composition. Together, these results demonstrate the expressive advantage of MuRA in learning complex multi-hop computations that remain challenging for existing hybrid architectures.

5 Related Work

Efficient sequence models and shared attention memory.

Reducing the computational cost of full attention has motivated extensive research into efficient sequence architectures. Early work explored sparse attention [7; 2; 48], while subsequent approaches developed efficient recurrent layers  [19; 18; 46]. These architectures were later incorporated into hybrid architectures that combine them with full attention, including Kimi K3 [40], Gemma 3 [16], Jamba [24], and OLMo Hybrid [27]. These architectures typically maintain separate memory for their efficient layers, however recent work explores the idea of memory sharing: Cross-Layer Attention [5] shares KV activations across layers, while DART [34] attends to compressed recurrent chunk states. Both reduce memory requirements but still attend over a growing number of entries. HySparse and HySparse2 [13; 43] instead reuse full-attention KV caches for bounded sparse retrieval. Closely related to our work, Graph Machine [20] also employs multi-hop sparse retrieval, but maintains learned weighted edges and updates KV representations across sparse layers, limiting its memory savings. In contrast, MuRA performs retrieval over a fixed attention graph, reusing the original KV cache across all sparse layers.

Expressivity of sequence models.

The expressive power of sequence models has been extensively studied, with circuit-complexity analyses establishing limitations of log-precision Transformers [29] and showing how recurrent depth, padding, and chain of though improve these limitations  [10; 26; 30]. Other work investigates the architectural resources required for tasks such as sparse averaging, Match3, and function composition [36; 37; 33; 6; 22]. Related analyses study limitations of linear RNNs [28; 38], with architectural modifications such as negative transition eigenvalues improving their state-tracking capabilities [17]. More recently, Merrill et al. [27] established expressive advantages of combining attention and recurrence, connecting these theoretical findings to the design of a large-scale hybrid model. Closely related to our work, Ye et al. [47] established lower bounds for hybrid architectures on sequential function composition, including architectures with multiple full-attention layers. While our analysis focuses on a single full-attention block, we establish a stronger capacity lower bound that allows arbitrary recurrent depth and extends to fixed top-κ\kappa shared-memory access.

6 Conclusion

We studied how sharing attention memory can enhance the expressive power of hybrid blocks without increasing their asymptotic computational or memory complexity. Using function composition as a model of multi-hop reasoning, we first established capacity lower bounds for existing hybrid blocks with either no KV-cache access or fixed top-κ\kappa retrieval, revealing fundamental limitations of these architectures. To overcome these limitations, we introduced MuRA, a simple yet powerful extension that enables multi-hop retrieval from a shared KV cache. Our theoretical results establish a strict expressivity hierarchy in retrieval depth: mm hops suffice to compute mm-function composition with constant width and logarithmic capacity, whereas computing (m+1)(m+1)-function composition with only mm hops requires polynomial capacity. Synthetic experiments with comparable retrieval budgets support this hierarchy and demonstrate the expressive advantages of MuRA over existing hybrid architectures. Together, our findings highlight retrieval depth as a fundamental architectural principle for designing more expressive hybrid language models.

Appendix A Additional Preliminaries

Notation.

We retain the notation of the main text and introduce new conventions, which will be helpful for the proofs below. The vectors 𝒆1,…,𝒆m{\bm{e}}_{1},\dots,{\bm{e}}_{m} represent the standard basis, with dimension specified where it is used, and 𝟎b\mathbf{0}_{b} is the zero vector in ℝb{\mathbb{R}}^{b}. The indicator of a set EE is 𝟙E\mathbbm{1}_{E}. We write dh=d/hd_{h}=d/h for the dimension of an attention head. In the communication proofs, 𝒛t{\bm{z}}_{t} denotes the representation at position tt immediately before full attention, and 𝒒tj,𝒌tj,𝒗tj{\bm{q}}_{t}^{j},{\bm{k}}_{t}^{j},{\bm{v}}_{t}^{j} are its original query, key, and value in head jj. These original vectors, and the neighborhoods determined by the full-attention scores αi,t(j)\alpha_{i,t}^{(j)}, remain fixed throughout subsequent shared-cache computations. The notation Topj,k⁡(u,T)\operatorname{Top}_{j,k}(u;T) denotes the highest scoring min⁡{k,|T|}\min\{k,|T|\} positions in T⊆[u−1]T\subseteq[u-1], ranked by decreasing score and then decreasing position with respect to query qujq_{u}^{j}.

Sequence modeling: embedding and decoding.

Throughout this paper, we consider hybrid blocks which take as input sequences 𝒂=(a1,…,aN){\bm{a}}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}) where each sequence element takes value in a finite alphabet ai∈[n]∀i∈[N]a_{i}\in[n]\quad\forall i\in[N]. The hybrid block then predicts an output token a^∈[n]\hat{a}\in[n]. This is done through two additional components to the hybrid block, the embedding and unembedding layers. An embedding layer 𝖤n:[n]×ℕ→ℝd\mathsf{E}_{n}:[n]\times{\mathbb{N}}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{d} produces

𝖤n​(𝒂)=[𝖤n​(a1,1),…,𝖤n​(aN,N)]⊤.\mathsf{E}_{n}({\bm{a}})=[\mathsf{E}_{n}(a_{1},1),\ldots,\mathsf{E}_{n}(a_{N},N)]^{\top}. (16)

At position tt, this embedding depends only on ata_{t}, and tt. Applying a block 𝖡\mathsf{B} gives 𝒀=𝖡⁡(𝖤n​(𝒂))=[𝒚1,…,𝒚N]⊤{\bm{Y}}=\mathsf{B}(\mathsf{E}_{n}({\bm{a}}))=[{\bm{y}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{y}}_{N}]^{\top}. An unembedding layer 𝖴n:ℝd→ℝn\mathsf{U}_{n}:{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{n} then produces output logits. The predicted symbol is

a^=arg​maxa∈[n]⁡[𝖬𝖫𝖯n​(𝐲N)]a.\widehat{a}=\argmax_{a\in[n]}[\mathsf{MLP}_{n}({\bm{y}}_{N})]_{a}. (17)

In practice, the embedding layer typically combines learned token embeddings with positional encodings:

𝖤n​(ai,i)=𝒗ai+𝒑i,\mathsf{E}_{n}(a_{i},i)={\bm{v}}_{a_{i}}+{\bm{p}}_{i}, (18)

where 𝒗ai∈ℝd{\bm{v}}_{a_{i}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} is the learned embedding of token aia_{i} and 𝒑i∈ℝd{\bm{p}}_{i}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} is a positional encoding, such as a sinusoidal encoding. Similarly, the unembedding layer is typically a linear projection. In this manuscript, we leave both maps unrestricted, as our lower bounds hold in this more general setting. For our upper-bound construction (Theorem 3.3), the required embedding maps can be implemented using standard embeddings followed by a single additional pre-attention recurrent layer, while retaining a linear unembedding.

Normalization and feed-forward networks.

In practice, sequence layers are typically augmented with layer normalization and position-wise feed-forward networks (FFNs), which we omit from our theoretical formulations for simplicity. Specifically, given an input sequence 𝑿=[𝒙1,…,𝒙N]⊤∈ℝN×d{\bm{X}}=[{\bm{x}}_{1},\dots,{\bm{x}}_{N}]^{\top}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N\times d} and a sequence layer 𝖫\mathsf{L}, we apply the following pre-normalization updates:

𝒁\displaystyle{\bm{Z}} =LN1⁡(𝑿),\displaystyle=\operatorname{LN}_{1}({\bm{X}}), (19)
𝑿~\displaystyle\widetilde{{\bm{X}}} =𝑿+𝖫⁡(𝒁),\displaystyle={\bm{X}}+\mathsf{L}({\bm{Z}}),
𝒀\displaystyle{\bm{Y}} =𝑿~+FFN⁡(LN2⁡(𝑿~)).\displaystyle=\widetilde{{\bm{X}}}+\operatorname{FFN}(\operatorname{LN}_{2}(\widetilde{{\bm{X}}})).

We use this structure throughout our experiments. In our theoretical analysis, we omit these components, as they operate independently at each token and can be incorporated into the unrestricted computations of the recurrent layers used by all hybrid models, without affecting the communication-based lower bounds.

Finite precision and attention arithmetic.

Throughout our analysis, hybrid blocks operate at finite precision p=p⁡(N)p=p(N), specifying the number of bits available to represent each scalar. Two common choices are constant precision, reflecting the fixed numerical precision used in practice, and logarithmic precision p=Θ⁡(log⁡N)p=\Theta(\log N), which is sufficient to distinguish token positions while limiting the information encoded in each scalar.

Since the order of arithmetic operations can affect finite-precision computations, we explicitly specify how attention is evaluated. For each query position uu and head jj, we first compute the query–key dot products by summing coordinate-wise products in a fixed order, obtaining the quantized pre-softmax logits γu,t(j)\gamma_{u,t}^{(j)}. We then apply a fixed positive, quantized exponential Expp\operatorname{Exp}_{p} to obtain the unnormalized attention weights

wu,t(j)=Expp⁡(γu,t(j)).w_{u,t}^{(j)}=\operatorname{Exp}_{p}(\gamma_{u,t}^{(j)}). (20)

For any set of positions T⊆[u]T\subseteq[u], we define the partial unnormalized attention sum and normalization factor as

𝒔j​(u,T)\displaystyle{\bm{s}}_{j}(u;T) =∑t∈TQuantp⁡(wu,t(j)​𝒗tj),\displaystyle=\sum_{t\in T}\operatorname{Quant}_{p}(w_{u,t}^{(j)}{\bm{v}}_{t}^{j}), (21)
Dj​(u,T)\displaystyle D_{j}(u;T) =∑t∈Twu,t(j).\displaystyle=\sum_{t\in T}w_{u,t}^{(j)}.

Here, Quantp\operatorname{Quant}_{p} denotes quantization to the prescribed precision, applied to each product before accumulation. The attention output is then computed by normalizing the accumulated sum:

Quantp⁡(𝒔j​(u,T)Dj​(u,T)).\operatorname{Quant}_{p}\left(\frac{{\bm{s}}_{j}(u;T)}{D_{j}(u;T)}\right). (22)

In particular, for disjoint sets T1,T2⊆[u]T_{1},T_{2}\subseteq[u], exact accumulation ensures

𝒔j​(u,T1∪T2)\displaystyle{\bm{s}}_{j}(u;T_{1}\cup T_{2}) =𝒔j​(u,T1)+𝒔j​(u,T2),\displaystyle={\bm{s}}_{j}(u;T_{1})+{\bm{s}}_{j}(u;T_{2}), (23)
Dj​(u,T1∪T2)\displaystyle D_{j}(u;T_{1}\cup T_{2}) =Dj​(u,T1)+Dj​(u,T2).\displaystyle=D_{j}(u;T_{1})+D_{j}(u;T_{2}).

Thus, independently computed partial statistics can be combined to reproduce the attention output exactly, as required by our communication protocols. This convention applies to both full and sparse attention throughout our proofs..

Common hidden width and recurrent memory.

For simplicity, the main text uses a common width dd for token representations and recurrent states. An implementation may instead have token width d0d_{0} and a larger persistent state. For example, sliding-window attention with a fixed window of ww predecessors can retain their keys and values in a state with 2​w​d02wd_{0} coordinates, together with a constant amount of indexing information. Kernel-based linear attention with feature dimension rr retains a feature–value accumulator and a feature sum, with r​d0+rrd_{0}+r coordinates for a single head [Katharopoulos et al., 2020]. For fixed ww, or fixed rr, these sizes are constant multiples of d0d_{0}, independent of sequence length. For the usual choice r=d0r=d_{0} in a single head, however, linear attention has a state quadratic in d0d_{0}; this cost must also be counted.

To realize these implementations within the main-text definitions, choose dd large enough for every token representation and every layer’s complete persistent state, and divisible by the head count. Pad smaller representations and states with zeros, and extend each map by restricting its input to the original coordinates and padding its output.

Appendix B Theorem proofs

Communication lower bound used in the proofs.

We use the deterministic consequence of Viola and Wigderson [2009, Theorem 3.2]: for fixed q≥2q\geq 2, the one-way (q+1)(q+1)-player protocol in the main text needs Ωq​(n1/q)\Omega_{q}(n^{1/q}) bits to compute qq-function composition. To match its table formulation to tree pointer jumping, take b=⌊n1/q⌋b=\lfloor n^{1/q}\rfloor and a bb-ary tree with qq pointer choices and Boolean leaf labels. Index the nodes at each depth injectively in [n][n], since there are at most bq≤nb^{q}\leq n of them. Encode the root choice by xx, the remaining pointer maps by fq,…,f2f_{q},\ldots,f_{2}, and the leaf labels by f1f_{1}, using output symbols 1,21,2. Assign fixed public values to unused table entries. This preserves each player’s hidden input and the speaking order. A composition protocol therefore solves the tree problem. Announcing its decoded Boolean output adds one bit, reconciling the source’s charged-output convention. The tree lower bound is Ωq​(b)\Omega_{q}(b), giving the required bound.

B.1 Proof of Theorem 2.7

Proof.

Set f3,…,fmf_{3},\ldots,f_{m} to the identity when m>2m>2. On the resulting input of length N=m​n+1N=mn+1, the required output is f1​(f2​(x))f_{1}(f_{2}(x)). We construct the three-player protocol of Definition 2.6: P3P_{3} knows f1,f2f_{1},f_{2} but not xx; P2P_{2} knows f1,xf_{1},x but not f2f_{2}; and P1P_{1} knows f2,xf_{2},x but not f1f_{1}. The model, embedding, decoder, All identity-table tokens, and task parameters are public. Messages are broadcast in the order P3→P2→P1P_{3}\to P_{2}\to P_{1}.

Player P3P_{3}: communicating boundary states.

Write 𝒉tpre,ℓ{\bm{h}}_{t}^{\mathrm{pre},\ell} and 𝒉tpost,ℓ{\bm{h}}_{t}^{\mathrm{post},\ell} for the recurrent states after position tt in layer ℓ\ell of the respective stacks. P3P_{3} is able to evaluate the entire block on positions 1,…,N−11,\ldots,N-1, without knowing xx. It broadcasts

(𝒉npre,Lpre,𝒉N−1pre,Lpre)(𝒉N−1post,ℓ)ℓ∈[Lpost].\left({\bm{h}}_{n}^{\mathrm{pre},{L_{\mathrm{pre}}}},{\bm{h}}_{N-1}^{\mathrm{pre},{L_{\mathrm{pre}}}}\right)\qquad\left({\bm{h}}_{N-1}^{\mathrm{post},\ell}\right)_{\ell\in[L_{\mathrm{post}}]}. (24)

These messages require p​d​(2+Lpost)pd(2+L_{\mathrm{post}}) bits. The transmitted pre-attention states allow subsequent players who know xx to compute its pre-attention representation 𝒛N{\bm{z}}_{N}, and players who know f2,xf_{2},x but not f1f_{1} to reconstruct the pre-attention representations 𝒛n+1,…,𝒛N{\bm{z}}_{n+1},\ldots,{\bm{z}}_{N}. Moreover, once the attention output at position NN has been recovered, the post-attention states at position N−1N-1 allow the final player to complete the forward pass.

Player P2P_{2}: partial attention and candidate records.

Using its knowledge of f1f_{1}, player P2P_{2} first computes the pre attention representations 𝒛t{\bm{z}}_{t}, as well as all key and value vectors for t∈[n]t\in[n]. From the boundary states at N−1N-1 and its knowledge of xx, it also computes 𝒛N{\bm{z}}_{N} and the final queries 𝒒Nj{\bm{q}}_{N}^{j} for every head. For each head jj, it broadcasts

𝒔j​(N,[n]),Dj​(N,[n]){\bm{s}}_{j}(N;[n]),\qquad D_{j}(N;[n]) (25)

defined in equation 21, costing p⁡(d+h)p(d+h) bits in total. It additionally selects

Tj=Topj,κ⁡(N;[n])T_{j}=\operatorname{Top}_{j,\kappa}(N;[n]) (26)

and transmits, for each t∈Tjt\in T_{j}, the record (𝒌tj,𝒗tj,αt,Nj)({\bm{k}}_{t}^{j},{\bm{v}}_{t}^{j},\alpha^{j}_{t,N}) costing a total of 2​p​(d+h)​min⁡{κ,n}2p(d+h)\min\{\kappa,n\} bits.

Player P1P_{1}: reconstructing full attention and top-κ\kappa access.

Starting from the pre-attention boundary states 𝒉npre,Lpre{\bm{h}}_{n}^{\mathrm{pre},{L_{\mathrm{pre}}}}, player P1P_{1} evaluates the pre-attention representations 𝒛i{\bm{z}}_{i} for n+1,…,Nn+1,\ldots,N. This suffix consists of f2f_{2}, the public identity tables, and xx. It also obtains every suffix key and value together with the final queries 𝒒Nj{\bm{q}}^{j}_{N} in the same way they were computed by P2P_{2}. For each head, it computes 𝒔j​(N,{n+1,…,N}){\bm{s}}_{j}(N;\{n+1,\ldots,N\}) and Dj​(N,{n+1,…,N})D_{j}(N;\{n+1,\ldots,N\}), adds the received prefix statistics, and normalizes with the model’s rounding rule. Equation 23 guarantees that this is the exact full-attention head output, including the final token’s self contribution. Writing 𝒐Nj∈ℝdh{\bm{o}}_{N}^{j}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d_{h}} for the reconstructed head-output column vector, it obtains

𝒙N(0)=𝒛N+𝑾O⊤​[𝒐N1𝒐Nh].{\bm{x}}_{N}^{(0)}={\bm{z}}_{N}+{\bm{W}}_{O}^{\top}\begin{bmatrix}{\bm{o}}_{N}^{1}\\ \vdots\\ {\bm{o}}_{N}^{h}\end{bmatrix}. (27)

Thus computing the representation of the final token xx after the attention layer.

For retrieval, it selects its own top-κ\kappa candidates among {n+1,…,N−1}\{n+1,\ldots,N-1\} and merges them with TjT_{j}. We use the following elementary identity, with all rankings following the same total order:

Topj,k⁡(u,A∪C)=Topj,k⁡(u,Topj,k⁡(u;A)∪Topj,k⁡(u;C))\operatorname{Top}_{j,k}(u;A\cup C)=\operatorname{Top}_{j,k}\bigl(u;\operatorname{Top}_{j,k}(u;A)\cup\operatorname{Top}_{j,k}(u;C)\bigr) (28)

for disjoint predecessor sets A,CA,C. Indeed, an element excluded from its own set’s top kk has at least kk elements of that set ranked ahead of it, and cannot be in the global top kk. This proves that the merge recovers every selected predecessor, including when scores tie or one side has fewer than kk elements. Adding the known self position NN recovers 𝒩j(κ)​(N)\mathcal{N}_{j}^{(\kappa)}(N) and all its keys and values.

Player P1P_{1} now advances the final token through the post-attention stack. Starting with 𝒙N(0){\bm{x}}_{N}^{(0)}, it knows at each layer the current token representation, that layer’s state at N−1N-1, and every entry of the fixed retrieved cache 𝑪N{\bm{C}}_{N}. It therefore applies the specified transition and output maps exactly. Induction over these layers recovers the block’s final representation, after which the public decoder outputs f1​(f2​(x))f_{1}(f_{2}(x)). No player needs the hidden table to execute its assigned computation.

Communication and the lower bound.

Since h≤dh\leq d The total cost is at most

p​d​(Lpost+2)+p⁡(d+h)+2​p​(d+h)​min⁡{κ,n}\displaystyle pd(L_{\mathrm{post}}+2)+p(d+h)+2p(d+h)\min\{\kappa,n\} (29)
≤p​d​(Lpost+2+4​κ).\displaystyle\leq pd(L_{\mathrm{post}}+2+4\kappa).

The three-player NOF lower bound stated in the main text requires Ω⁡(n)\Omega(\sqrt{n}) bits for two-function composition. Applying it to this exact simulation completes the proof. ∎

Remark: comparison with prior bounds and tightness.

Theorem 1.1 of Ye et al. [2026] studies a similar setting, considering multiple full-attention layers and a bounded number of recurrent layers between them. In their notation, taking L=2L=2 leaves one full-attention layer, permits up to 2122^{12} efficient layers after it, and gives a width–precision lower bound of N2−10=N1/1024N^{2^{-10}}=N^{1/1024}. Our Ω⁡(n)\Omega(\sqrt{n}) bound significantly improves this lower bound for the single hybrid block setting, applies to arbitrary post-attention recurrent depth with its state cost charged, and allows top-κ\kappa cache access.

We also highlight the role the of recurrent layers in the above bound. For a single attention layer without recurrence, the communication argument of Peng et al. [2024, Theorem 1] shows a stronger lower bound of Ω⁡(n​log⁡n)\Omega(n\log n) for two-function composition. The weaker Ω⁡(n)\Omega(\sqrt{n}) hybrid lower bound is consistent with RNNs providing an additional expressive advantage around a single attention layer. The tightness of our Ω⁡(n)\Omega(\sqrt{n}) lower bound remains an open question.

B.2 Proof of Theorem 3.3

Proof.

We construct an mm-hop block 𝖡𝜿\mathsf{B}_{\bm{\kappa}} with 𝜿=(1,…,1)\bm{\kappa}=(1,\ldots,1), h=1h=1, Lpre=0L_{\mathrm{pre}}=0, Lpost=1L_{\mathrm{post}}=1, and d=4​m+7d=4m+7 which solves mm- function composition.

Fix n≥2n\geq 2. Let tr,i=(r−1)​n+it_{r,i}=(r-1)n+i denote the position containing fr​(i)f_{r}(i), and let t⋆=m​n+1=Nt_{\star}=mn+1=N. In this proof, 𝒆1,…,𝒆m+1{\bm{e}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{e}}_{m+1} are the standard basis of ℝm+1{\mathbb{R}}^{m+1}, and we suppress the sole head index j=1j=1 in queries, keys, values, and neighborhoods.

Embedding the function tables and query.

We use the the following token embedding:

𝖤n​(fr​(i),tr,i)=[1ii2fr​(i)fr​(i)2𝒆rfr​(i)​𝒆r𝟎2​m],𝖤n​(x,t⋆)=[100xx2𝒆m+1x​𝒆m+1𝟎2​m].\mathsf{E}_{n}(f_{r}(i),t_{r,i})=\begin{bmatrix}1\\ i\\ i^{2}\\ f_{r}(i)\\ f_{r}(i)^{2}\\ {\bm{e}}_{r}\\ f_{r}(i){\bm{e}}_{r}\\ \mathbf{0}_{2m}\end{bmatrix},\qquad\mathsf{E}_{n}(x,t_{\star})=\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\\ 0\\ x\\ x^{2}\\ {\bm{e}}_{m+1}\\ x{\bm{e}}_{m+1}\\ \mathbf{0}_{2m}\end{bmatrix}. (30)

Both vectors have 5+2​(m+1)+2​m=4​m+75+2(m+1)+2m=4m+7 coordinates. These features depend only on the visible token and position; in particular, they do not reveal a function value at any other argument. The last 2​m2m coordinates are reserved for sparse-attention output.

Full attention layer 𝖠\mathsf{A}.

Let 𝑺∈ℝ(m+1)×(m+1){\bm{S}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{(m+1)\times(m+1)} be a linear map such that 𝑺​𝒆1=𝟎{\bm{S}}{\bm{e}}_{1}=\mathbf{0} and 𝑺​𝒆r=𝒆r−1{\bm{S}}{\bm{e}}_{r}={\bm{e}}_{r-1} for 2≤r≤m+12\leq r\leq m+1. Thus the sparse layer writes zmm+1,1m+1\frac{z_{m}}{m+1},\frac{1}{m+1} into workspace coordinates 2​m+8,2​m+92m+8,2m+9. Their input coordinates are zero, so the sparse layer’s residual adds no other contribution there.

For output symbol a∈[n]a\in[n], let row aa of 𝑼n{\bm{U}}_{n} have coefficients (2​a,−a2)(2a,-a^{2}) on those two workspace coordinates and zero elsewhere. Its ideal logit is

2​a​zmm+1−a2​1m+1=2​a​zm−a2m+1=zm2−(a−zm)2m+1.2a\frac{z_{m}}{m+1}-a^{2}\frac{1}{m+1}=\frac{2az_{m}-a^{2}}{m+1}=\frac{z_{m}^{2}-(a-z_{m})^{2}}{m+1}. (38)

Finite precision.

We show that the construction remains correct with p=O⁡(log⁡(m​n))p=O(\log(mn)) bits of precision per scalar. Choose a fixed-point format with dyadic grid spacing δ\delta satisfying

δ<min⁡{116​d,18​(m+1)​(n+1)2,164​N​d},\delta<\min\left\{\frac{1}{16\sqrt{d}},\frac{1}{8(m+1)(n+1)^{2}},\frac{1}{64N\sqrt{d}}\right\}, (39)

taking the largest dyadic spacing satisfying this inequality. All unscaled query–key dot products are integers and can be computed exactly. We approximate the attention scaling factor 1/d1/\sqrt{d} by a positive grid value cc with |c−1/d|≤δ|c-1/\sqrt{d}|\leq\delta. Since each correct retrieval position has unscaled score 11, while all competing positions have scores at most 00, rounding the scaled logits preserves a gap of at least c−2​δ>0c-2\delta>0.

We choose Expp\operatorname{Exp}_{p} to be the exponential rounded to the fixed-point grid, with saturation to [δ,4][\delta,4] and Expp⁡(0)=1\operatorname{Exp}_{p}(0)=1. The correct position consequently receives an unnormalized weight exceeding every competitor by at least 1/(2​d)1/(2\sqrt{d}). Since the normalization factor is at most 4​N4N, the corresponding normalized attention scores differ by at least 1/(8​N​d)1/(8N\sqrt{d}). The final constraint on δ\delta ensures that this ordering is preserved even after quantization of the normalized scores. Thus, all top-11 retrievals remain unchanged.

In the sparse-attention layer, all queries are zero, so every attention logit is exactly zero. Choosing Expp⁡(0)=1\operatorname{Exp}_{p}(0)=1 assigns equal weights to all m+1m+1 retrieved positions. Since their value coordinates are integers, the unnormalized attention sums and normalization factor are computed exactly. Quantization of the normalized output introduces an error of at most δ\delta in each workspace coordinate of equation 36. Consequently, exact accumulation of the decoder’s weighted sums, followed by final rounding, introduces an error of at most

(2​n+n2+1)​δ=(n+1)2​δ<18​(m+1)(2n+n^{2}+1)\delta=(n+1)^{2}\delta<\frac{1}{8(m+1)} (40)

in each output logit. Since the ideal logit gap is at least 1/(m+1)1/(m+1), the correct symbol remains the unique maximizer, ensuring exact decoding.

Finally, we verify that all intermediate computations fit within the claimed precision. Since Expp\operatorname{Exp}_{p} takes values in [δ,4][\delta,4] and value coordinates have magnitude at most nn, each quantized weighted-value coordinate has magnitude at most 4​n+δ4n+\delta. Accumulating up to NN terms therefore requires representing values of magnitude O⁡(n​N)=O⁡(m​n2)O(nN)=O(mn^{2}). All other intermediate quantities, including embeddings, routing products, and decoder products, have magnitude O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}). Moreover, the choice of δ\delta in equation 39 requires only O⁡(log⁡(m​n))O(\log(mn)) fractional bits. Thus, including integer bits and accumulation guard bits, p=O⁡(log⁡(m​n))p=O(\log(mn)) bits per scalar suffice. Since d=4​m+7d=4m+7, Lpre=0L_{\mathrm{pre}}=0, and Lpost=1L_{\mathrm{post}}=1, the construction has capacity C⁡(𝖡𝜿)=2​p​d=O⁡(m​log⁡(m​n))C(\mathsf{B}_{\bm{\kappa}})=2pd=O(m\log(mn)), which reduces to O⁡(log⁡N)O(\log N) for fixed mm.

B.3 Proof of Theorem 3.4

Proof.

Let N=(m+1)​n+1N=(m+1)n+1, and assume 𝖡𝜿\mathsf{B}_{\bm{\kappa}} is a 𝜿\bm{\kappa}-MuRA block that is able to solve qq-function composition, where 𝜿∈ℕm\bm{\kappa}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{m}. We generalize the proof of Theorem 2.7, and show that there exists a (m+2)(m+2)-player NOF protocol (Definition 2.6) that is able to simulate the forward pass of 𝖡𝜿\mathsf{B}_{\bm{\kappa}}, with commmunication complexity C⁡(𝖡𝜿)C(\mathsf{B}_{\bm{\kappa}}). The proof then follows from the classic m+2m+2-player NOF protocol communication bound Ω⁡(n1m+1)\Omega({n^{\frac{1}{m+1}}}) Viola and Wigderson [2009].

Player Pm+2P_{m+2}: communicating boundary states.

Write 𝒉tpre,ℓ{\bm{h}}_{t}^{\mathrm{pre},\ell} for the recurrent states after position tt in layer ℓ\ell of the pre attention recurrent layers. Similarly to the proof of Theorem 2.7, Pm+2P_{m+2} is able to evaluate the entire block on positions 1,…,N−11,\ldots,N-1, without knowing xx. It broadcasts

(𝒉r​npre,Lpre)r∈[m+1].\left({\bm{h}}_{rn}^{\mathrm{pre},{L_{\mathrm{pre}}}}\right)_{r\in[m+1]}. (41)

These messages require p​d​(m+1)pd(m+1) bits. The transmitted pre-attention states allow subsequent players who know f1,…,fr−1,fr+1,…,fN,xf_{1},\dots,f_{r-1},f_{r+1},\dots,f_{N},x, but not fif_{i}, to compute pre-attention representations 𝒛t{\bm{z}}_{t}, for t=1,…​n​(r−1),n​r+1,…,Nt=1,\dots n(r-1),nr+1,\dots,N.

The following communication steps are used to construct two main quantities needed for the last player P1P_{1} to complete the forward pass, the full attention computation, and the retrieval set. For clarity, we present these two computations separately, but note that they happen in parallel, each player filling its role in each of the computations simultaniously.

Full attention computation: Using its knowledge of f1,…,fmf_{1},\dots,f_{m}, player Pm+1P_{m+1} first computes the pre attention representations 𝒛t{\bm{z}}_{t}, as well as all key and value vectors for t∈[m​n]t\in[mn]. From the boundary states at N−1N-1 and its knowledge of xx, it also computes 𝒛N{\bm{z}}_{N} and the final queries 𝒒Nj{\bm{q}}_{N}^{j} for every head. For each head jj, it broadcasts

𝒔j​(N,[m​n]),Dj​(N,[m​n]){\bm{s}}_{j}(N;[mn]),\qquad D_{j}(N;[mn]) (42)

Starting from the pre-attention boundary states 𝒉m​npre,Lpre{\bm{h}}_{mn}^{\mathrm{pre},{L_{\mathrm{pre}}}}, player PmP_{m} evaluates the pre-attention representations 𝒛i{\bm{z}}_{i} for m​n+1,…,Nmn+1,\ldots,N. This suffix consists of fm+1f_{m+1} and xx. It then computes every key and value vector from this suffix, together with the final queries 𝒒Nj{\bm{q}}^{j}_{N}. For each head, it computes 𝒔j​(N,{n​m+1,…,N}){\bm{s}}_{j}(N;\{nm+1,\ldots,N\}) and Dj​(N,{n​m+1,…,N})D_{j}(N;\{nm+1,\ldots,N\}), adds the received prefix statistics, and normalizes with the model’s rounding rule. Equation 23 guarantees that this is the exact full-attention head output, including the final token’s self contribution. 𝒙N(0)=𝒛N+𝑾O⊤​[𝒐N1𝒐Nh].{\bm{x}}_{N}^{(0)}={\bm{z}}_{N}+{\bm{W}}_{O}^{\top}\begin{bmatrix}{\bm{o}}_{N}^{1}\\ \vdots\\ {\bm{o}}_{N}^{h}\end{bmatrix}. (43)

Thus computing the representation of the final token xx after the attention layer. The total communication cost of this process is p⁡(d+h)p(d+h).

Rj​(t)=(t,𝒒tj,𝒌tj,𝒗tj).R_{j}(t)=(t,{\bm{q}}_{t}^{j},{\bm{k}}_{t}^{j},{\bm{v}}_{t}^{j}). (44)

brec=3​p​(d/h+1).b_{\mathrm{rec}}=3p(d/h+1). (45)

Additionally, define recursively for r∈[m]\quad r\in[m],

Fj,0\displaystyle F_{j,0} =Gj,0={N},\displaystyle=G_{j,0}=\{N\}, (46)
Fj,r\displaystyle F_{j,r} ={t∈Topj,κr⁡(s;[N])∣s∈Fj,r−1},\displaystyle=\bigl\{t\in\operatorname{Top}_{j,\kappa_{r}}(s;[N])\mid s\in F_{j,r-1}\bigr\},

The auxiliary set Gj,rG_{j,r} contains the candidates obtained at the rr-th hop when positions corresponding to the function table frf_{r} are excluded from retrieval.

Since P1P_{1} can also reconstruct the full-attention output, as shown above, and knows the query xx, it can complete the remaining forward pass and produce the correct output, completing the proof.

The base case i=m+1i=m+1 is simple. As shown above, player Pm+1P_{m+1} can compute the final pre-attention representation 𝒛N{\bm{z}}_{N} and hence the record Rj​(N)R_{j}(N) for every head j∈[h]j\in[h]. For the inductive step, suppose player PiP_{i} receives from Pi+1P_{i+1} the sets Fj,m−iF_{j,m-i} and Gj,m−i+1G_{j,m-i+1}, together with their corresponding token records. Write r=m+1−ir=m+1-i, and let Sr=[n​r+1,…,n⁡(r+1)]S_{r}=[nr+1,\dots,n(r+1)] denote the positions of the function table excluded in the definition of Gj,rG_{j,r}. To recover Fj,rF_{j,r}, player PiP_{i} computes, for each s∈Fj,r−1s\in F_{j,r-1}, the top-κr\kappa_{r} candidates within BrB_{r}. Topj,k⁡(s,A∪B)=Topj,k⁡(s,Topj,k⁡(s;A)∪Topj,k⁡(s;B)),\operatorname{Top}_{j,k}(s;A\cup B)=\operatorname{Top}_{j,k}\bigl(s;\operatorname{Top}_{j,k}(s;A)\cup\operatorname{Top}_{j,k}(s;B)\bigr), (47)

which holds for disjoint sets A,BA,B under consistent tie-breaking.

Having recovered Fj,rF_{j,r} and its corresponding records, player PiP_{i} computes Gj,r+1G_{j,r+1} by selecting the top-κr+1\kappa_{r+1} candidates for each s∈Fj,rs\in F_{j,r}, excluding the function table unavailable to PiP_{i}. Since all remaining tokens are known to this player, their representations and attention scores can be computed using the transmitted boundary states. At each retrieval hop r∈[m]r\in[m], the transmitted records require at most 3​p​(d+h)​∏ℓ=1rκℓ3p(d+h)\prod_{\ell=1}^{r}\kappa_{\ell} bits. Since κℓ≥1\kappa_{\ell}\geq 1 for all ℓ\ell, including the initial messages gives a total communication cost of at most

d​p​(m+1)+(d+h)​p+3​p​(d+h)​m​∏ℓ=1mκℓ=O⁡(C⁡(𝖡𝜿)),dp(m+1)+(d+h)p+3p(d+h)m\prod_{\ell=1}^{m}\kappa_{\ell}=O(C(\mathsf{B}_{\bm{\kappa}})), (48)

where the last equality holds, using h≤dh\leq d.
