Appendix C Experimental details

We provide the implementation and training details of our synthetic experiments below. All experiments were conducted on NVIDIA L40 GPUs using Python 3.11.16, PyTorch 2.12.1+cu126, CUDA 12.6, and NumPy 2.4.6.

C.1 Dataset and Causal Supervision

Sampling and serialization.

Each example consists of five functions f1,…,f5:[n]→[n]f_{1},\ldots,f_{5}:[n]\to[n], where nn is sampled from {25,…,30}\{25,\ldots,30\}. Conditional on nn, all 5​n5n function values are sampled independently and uniformly from [n][n]. The functions are serialized as

(BOS,f1​(1),…,f1​(n),…,f5​(1),…,f5​(n)).\bigl(\mathrm{BOS},f_{1}(1),\ldots,f_{1}(n),\ldots,f_{5}(1),\ldots,f_{5}(n)\bigr). (49)

Unlike Definition 2.5, the sequence begins with a beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token and contains no explicit final query xx. Function tables appear in increasing order, without separator tokens, yielding a sequence length of N=5​n+1∈[126,151]N=5n+1\in[126,151].

The dataset contains 250,000 independently generated examples, divided into 200,000 training, 25,000 validation, and 25,000 test examples. Each split is stratified by nn, with the number of examples for any two domain sizes differing by at most one. During batching, each example occupies a separate row, and shorter sequences are right-padded. Padding positions are excluded from attention, retrieval, loss computation, and accuracy evaluation.

Targets and loss.

We evaluate the ability of hybrid blocks to compute function compositions of depths r∈[4]r\in[4] using causal supervision at multiple positions. Specifically, each token containing fi​(j)f_{i}(j), for i∈{2,…,5}i\in\{2,\ldots,5\}, is assigned i−1i-1 targets, corresponding to compositions of depths r∈[i−1]r\in[i-1]:

zi,j,r=(fi−r∘⋯∘fi−1)(fi(j)).z_{i,j,r}=(f_{i-r}\circ\cdots\circ f_{i-1})(f_{i}(j)). (50)

Thus, tokens from the second function table predict f1​(f2​(j))f_{1}(f_{2}(j)), while tokens from later tables are supervised at progressively greater depths. The BOS token and the first function table receive no direct supervision.

Each depth r∈[4]r\in[4] has a separate linear readout applied to the corresponding token representations, producing 30 output logits. For examples with n<30n<30, logits corresponding to symbols outside [n][n] are masked, and each token is evaluated only at depths for which a target is defined. Consequently, each example contributes n⁡(5−r)n(5-r) targets at depth rr, for a total of 10​n10n supervised predictions.

All valid predictions contribute equally to the training objective. Denoting by 𝒮ℬ\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{B}} the set of supervised example–position–target triples in a logical batch ℬ\mathcal{B}, we minimize

ℒℬ=−1|𝒮ℬ|∑(e,p,t)∈𝒮ℬlnpr(t∣e,p),\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{B}}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{B}}|}\sum_{(e,p,t)\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{B}}}\ln p_{r}(t\mid e,p), (51)

where prp_{r} is the masked softmax distribution produced by readout rr, and tt is its target at the corresponding example, position and composition depth rr.

C.2 Hybrid Block Architecture

Token embedding map.

All models use a token embedding scheme inspired by Kozachinskiy et al. [2025], consisting of nine deterministic features followed by a learned affine projection to width d=16d=16. With the BOS token at position 11, each subsequent token at position t∈{2,…,N}t\in\{2,\ldots,N\} is characterized by its function argument i=1+((t−2)modn)i=1+((t-2)\bmod n), function-table index b=1+⌊(t−2)/n⌋b=1+\lfloor(t-2)/n\rfloor, and token value v∈[n]v\in[n].

Define the circular encoding

𝒄R​(a)=(cos⁡2​π​(a−1)R,sin⁡2​π​(a−1)R)⊤,Rn=n+1.{\bm{c}}_{R}(a)=\left(\cos\frac{2\pi(a-1)}{R},\sin\frac{2\pi(a-1)}{R}\right)^{\top},\qquad R_{n}=n+1. (52)

The nine input features are given by

ϕ(t,v)=[\displaystyle\bm{\phi}(t,v)=\bigl[ Rn​𝒄Rn​(v)⊤,Rn​𝒄Rn​(i)⊤,\displaystyle R_{n}{\bm{c}}_{R_{n}}(v)^{\top},\ R_{n}{\bm{c}}_{R_{n}}(i)^{\top}, (53)
5𝒄5(b+1)⊤, 5𝒄5(b)⊤, 1]⊤.\displaystyle 5{\bm{c}}_{5}(b+1)^{\top},\ 5{\bm{c}}_{5}(b)^{\top},\ 1\bigr]^{\top}.

The two function-table encodings use offsets b+1b+1 and bb, respectively. The BOS token is assigned the feature vector (0,0,0,0,5​Rn,0,0,0,1)⊤(0,0,0,0,5R_{n},0,0,0,1)^{\top}, while padding tokens receive zero features. All feature vectors are mapped to ℝ16{\mathbb{R}}^{16} by a learned affine transformation, with padding positions masked again afterward to eliminate the effect of the bias.

This encoding provides the function-table index, argument, and value of each token without revealing composition paths or targets. We use no additional learned token or function embeddings, absolute positional embeddings, or rotary positional transformations.

Layers.

Each hybrid block consists of one full-attention layer followed by four efficient sequence layers, implemented as recurrent or sparse-attention layers depending on the architecture. All layers have width d=16d=16, and use four heads. As described in Appendix A, each layer uses the pre-normalization and position-wise feed-forward structure of Equation 19. We use affine LayerNorm with ϵ=10−5\epsilon=10^{-5} and apply an additional affine LayerNorm before the output readouts. Similarly to Kozachinskiy et al. [2025], each of the five feed-forward networks has two hidden layers of width 6464, with SwiGLU activations, giving dimensions 16→64→64→1616\to 64\to 64\to 16. Both hidden layers use separate gate and value projections. All model parameters use standard initialization.

MuRA retrieval.

To evaluate the effect of retrieval depth, we consider four MuRA configurations with retrieval widths 𝜿=(32)\bm{\kappa}=(32), (16,1)(16,1), (11,1,1)(11,1,1), and (8,1,1,1)(8,1,1,1), corresponding to depths one through four. These configurations have matched retrieval budgets of 32 tokens across all hops, except for (11,1,1)(11,1,1), which retrieves up to 33 tokens.

Each MuRA layer has four attention heads, with retrieval depths assigned to encourage learning compositions of different orders. Specifically, for a configuration 𝜿=(κ1,…,κm)\bm{\kappa}=(\kappa_{1},\ldots,\kappa_{m}), head j∈[4]j\in[4] uses retrieval widths (κ1,…,κmin⁡(j,m))(\kappa_{1},\ldots,\kappa_{\min(j,m)}) and attends only to positions reached after exactly min⁡(j,m)\min(j,m) hops. Thus, successive heads perform increasingly deep retrievals, up to the maximum depth mm. This assignment is repeated across all four MuRA layers. Routing decisions are detached from the computational graph, while gradients continue to flow through the selected keys and values.

Hybrid block baselines.

We compare MuRA against four hybrid block baselines: kernel-based linear attention [Katharopoulos et al., 2020], sliding-window attention [Beltagy et al., 2020], Gated DeltaNet [Yang et al., 2024], and a simplified HySparse variant [Gao et al., 2026], equivalent to one-hop MuRA with 𝜿=(32)\bm{\kappa}=(32). For a fair comparison, all architectures use the same width d=16d=16, one full-attention layer, and four subsequent efficient sequence layers, with four attention heads where applicable.

For sliding-window attention, we evaluate two window sizes, 32 and 16. The former matches the retrieval budget of MuRA but incurs greater memory and computational overhead, since each of the four sliding-window layers maintains its own KV cache. In our short-sequence setting, these caches collectively store approximately as many KV entries as an additional full-attention layer. We therefore also evaluate a smaller window of size 16, providing a more computationally efficient baseline.

C.3 Optimization and Training Schedules

All models are trained for 500 epochs using AdamW with a batch size of 2,048, weight decay of 0.01, and optimizer parameters β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.999\beta_{2}=0.999, and ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}. The learning rate is linearly warmed up over the first 40 epochs to a peak of 10−310^{-3}, followed by cosine decay to one-tenth of the peak rate. After gradient accumulation, the global gradient ℓ2\ell_{2} norm is clipped to 1.0 before each optimization step.

Appendix D Extended related work

Efficient sequence models and shared attention memory.

Reducing the cost of full attention has motivated a range of efficient sequence architectures. Early approaches introduced sparse attention mechanisms [Child et al., 2019, Beltagy et al., 2020, Zaheer et al., 2020]; subsequent work developed recurrent and state-space architectures, including S4 [Gu et al., 2021], Mamba [Gu and Dao, 2023], and Gated DeltaNet [Yang et al., 2024]. These recurrent architectures support parallel training algorithms and maintain fixed-size states during autoregressive inference. Hybrid architectures combine efficient layers with periodic full attention, as in Kimi 3 [Team et al., 2026], Gemma 3 [Gemma Team and others, 2025], Jamba [Lieber et al., 2024], and OLMo Hybrid [Merrill et al., 2026]. Their efficient layers typically maintain memory independently of the full-attention KV cache. Recent work has explored sharing this memory. Cross-Layer Attention [Brandon et al., 2024] shares KV activations across attention layers, while DART [Qian et al., 2026] attends to compressed recurrent chunk states. These approaches reduce memory requirements, although each attention operation still accesses a number of entries that grows with sequence length. HySparse and HySparse2 [Gao et al., 2026, Wei et al., 2026] instead reuse a full-attention KV cache through bounded sparse retrieval in subsequent layers. Graph Machine [Hou, 2026], which is closely related to our work, also uses multi-hop sparse retrieval in hybrid architectures. It constructs and updates learned weighted edges across layers and operates on layer-specific representations. In MuRA, retrieval traverses a fixed attention graph; the subsequent sparse layers reuse the resulting neighborhoods and the original full-attention KV cache.

Expressivity as a guide to architecture design.

Prior work has examined sequence-model expressivity from several perspectives. Circuit-complexity analyses establish limitations of log-precision Transformers [Merrill and Sabharwal, 2023] and study how padding tokens[Merrill and Sabharwal, 2026], recurrent application of layers [Dehghani et al., 2018] and chain of thought tokens [Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024] expand their capabilities. Other studies analyze the resources required for tasks such as sparse averaging, 3-token Matching, and function composition [Sanford et al., 2023, Sanford et al., 2024, Peng et al., 2024, Chen et al., 2024, Kozachinskiy et al., 2025]. Limitations identified for shallow Transformers have also motivated mechanisms such as Strassen attention [Kozachinskiy et al., 2025]. Complementarily, Gelberg et al. [2026] study the relationship between Transformer representations and KV-cache compressibility, relating expressive capacity and memory requirements to the learned representations.

Beyond Transformers, analyses of linear RNNs identify limitations in state tracking [Merrill et al., 2024, Sarrof et al., 2024], while Grazzi et al. [2025] show that allowing negative transition eigenvalues can improve these capabilities. Merrill et al. [2026] establish expressive advantages of combining attention and recurrence, and connect these results to the design of a large-scale hybrid model. Closely related to our analysis, Ye et al. [2026] prove lower bounds for hybrid architectures on sequential function composition. We study a simpler composition task and obtain a stronger capacity lower bound for a single full-attention block, allowing arbitrary recurrent depth with its state budget accounted for as in Appendix B, as well as top-κ\kappa shared-memory access. Their framework also covers architectures with multiple full-attention layers. The comparison and the open question of tightness are discussed after the proof in Appendix B.1.

Expressivity analysis also guides architecture design for other structured data. Examples include graph neural networks [Xu et al., 2018, Morris et al., 2019, Bar-Shalom et al., 2024, Eitan et al., 2025a, Southern et al., 2025], topological neural networks [Bodnar et al., 2021, Eitan et al., 2025b], weight- and gradient-space architectures [Navon et al., 2023, Dayan et al., 2026, Gelberg et al., 2025], and permutation-invariant models for sets and sets of structured elements [Zaheer et al., 2017, Maron et al., 2020]. These studies use formal expressivity results to inform architectural choices that respect the structure and symmetries of their inputs.
